My whole life I've farmed this same land in Quzhou. I'm 70 years old now, my back isn't what it was, and my two sons are in the city. My wife still helps when she can. I have about 8 mu.

I don't need to think too hard about what to plant. Everyone here plants wheat in winter and corn in summer. That's what my father did. That's what works on this flat ground with our wells. I'm not going to try something new at my age — if it fails I have nothing to fall back on.

For wheat, I'll hire a neighbor with a rotary tiller to prepare the ground in October after I pull the corn. I'll buy improved seed from the village supply shop — same variety I've used the last few years, not the old seeds, those don't yield as well anymore. I'll put down one bag of diammonium phosphate per mu when I sow, and then come spring at jointing I'll spread urea on top. My grandson says I put on too much, but I've seen what a thin crop looks like, and I'm not willing to risk it. I'll pump water four times — once before the ground freezes, once at jointing, once when it heads out, and once more if it looks dry during grain fill.

After wheat harvest in June, I'll plant hybrid corn seed straight into the stubble — no need to till again, saves money and my knees. I'll apply fertilizer at planting and again when the corn is knee-high. Summer rains usually come, so I'll only pump water if it's dry early or late in the season.

For pesticides, I'll spray the wheat twice — herbicide early in spring, then something for rust and aphids before heading. Corn I'll spray once for stem borer and leaf blight if I see it.
